summary: Catalogs known TCP implementation problems with Path MTU Discovery, including the long-standing black hole problem and confusion between the maximum segment size and the path's packet size limits. It is informational and suggests fixes.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2923 describes three ways TCP can behave badly when Path MTU Discovery is in use. The problems can stop large transfers, delay acknowledgments or force later connections to use smaller segments than necessary.

subtitle: Three TCP implementation problems that can make Path MTU Discovery fail or perform poorly.

tldr.problem: Path MTU Discovery can fail when needed ICMP messages are blocked or missing. TCP implementations can also mishandle acknowledgments or advertise a segment size based on an earlier path limit.
tldr.mechanism: The memo catalogs black-hole detection, stretch acknowledgments and MSS selection, with descriptions, traces, detection advice and fixes for each problem.
tldr.outcome: It recommends that TCP adapt after repeated timeouts, acknowledge according to received segments and base the advertised MSS on interface MTUs. It is Informational.

today: RFC 2923 is Informational. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: A Checklist for TCP Problems
sections.content:
The memo covers three known TCP implementation problems related to Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD). It focuses on TCP behavior, not PMTUD issues in other upper-layer protocols or IPv6-specific issues.

For each problem, it gives a classification, explanation, example traces, a way to detect the issue and a suggested fix. The structure follows the problem descriptions in RFC 2525.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo uses the same checklist for each TCP problem: what happens, how to spot it and what an implementation can do about it.

sections.title: The PMTUD Black Hole
sections.content:
A sender sets the Don't Fragment bit when probing with a large packet. If a router cannot forward it, the router should send an ICMP Fragmentation Needed message. When that message is missing, large packets can disappear while smaller packets still pass.

The memo describes bulk transfers that repeatedly time out. After several timeouts, TCP should try smaller packets and may turn off PMTUD for a time, then probe again later. IPv6 has no DF bit; the memo notes its minimum supported MTU is 1280 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: Small packets may pass even when large ones vanish. If the warning never arrives, TCP should try smaller packets and later check whether the path has changed.

sections.title: Stretch Acknowledgments
sections.content:
A receiver that waits for every second full-sized segment may use the advertised MSS to decide what counts as full-sized. PMTUD can make actual segments much smaller, so acknowledgments then arrive less often than intended.

The memo calls these stretch ACKs and says they can encourage bursty traffic and impede congestion-window growth. Suggested fixes are to acknowledge every other packet regardless of size or to track the size of received segments.
sections.plainLanguage: If the receiver counts bytes using an outdated segment size, it may wait too long before acknowledging data. It should count received packets or learn their actual size.

sections.title: Choosing the Advertised MSS
sections.content:
The advertised Maximum Segment Size (MSS) tells the remote host the largest TCP segment the local system can receive. The memo says this value should be based on the MTUs of the system's interfaces, not on a PMTU learned for an earlier connection.

An earlier path limit may be smaller than the local system can receive, and a later return path may differ. Advertising an unnecessarily small MSS can reduce performance and prevent later probing for a larger path MTU.
sections.plainLanguage: Tell the other host what your own interfaces can receive. Do not carry a small limit from an earlier route into a new connection.

sections.title: ICMP Filtering and Security
sections.content:
The security discussion notes that strict firewall filtering can block ICMP messages needed by PMTUD. The memo asks designers and deployers of security systems to understand how filtering affects higher-level protocols.

It argues that fixing ICMP black holes is preferable to relying on every TCP implementation to work around them.
sections.plainLanguage: Blocking every ICMP message can break normal TCP transfers. Firewalls need to allow the ICMP responses that a permitted connection depends on.
